articles.content: 본문 국제일반 대만 매체 “앨리스 황은 중국 정보기관 반도체팀 소속” 조해영 기자 수정 2026-11-14 21:37 펼침 0:00 Your browser does not support the audio element. 지난해 5월22일 대만 타이베이의 한 식당에서 엔비디아 최고경영자(CEO) 젠슨 황(왼쪽)이 주최한 만찬에 싱가포르 기업 임원인 앨리스 황(오른쪽)이 앉아 있다. 사진은 대만방송 시티아이(CTI)의 화면을 갈무리한 것이다. 타이베이/AFP 연합뉴스 젠슨 황 전 엔비디아 최고경영자(CEO)의 혼외 관계 상대로 지목된 앨리스 황(중국명 황러)가 중국 정보기관의 반도체 전담 조직 소속이었다는 보도가 나왔다. 대만 자유시보는 11일(현지시각) 미국 소식통을 인용해 앨리스 황이 중국 국가안전부의 ‘반도체팀’ 소속이었다고 보도했다. 보도에 따르면 중국공산당 중앙판공청은 국가안전부를 포함해 중앙과학기술위원회, 국가인터넷정보판공실, 상무부, 통일전선공작부, 인민해방군 관련 부서 등이 참여하는 인공지능(AI) 관련 조직을 만들었다. 이 조직은 미국 내 데이터센터 건설 반대 여론 조성, 반도체 수출 규제 완화를 위한 로비 등의 활동을 해왔다고 자유시보는 전했다. 보도에 따르면 앨리스 황은 이 가운데 국가안전부 내부의 반도체팀에 소속돼 있었으며, 제3국에 페이퍼컴퍼니를 만들어 반도체와 고성능 서버를 사들이고 젠슨 황에게 접근해 미국이 반도체 수출 규제를 완화하도록 하는 임무를 맡았다. 앨리스 황은 국가안전부장으로부터 직접 지휘를 받았으며, 앨리스 황과 비슷한 임무를 수행하는 여성 요원이 최소한 한 명 이상 존재하고 미국의 주요 기술 대기업에서 활동하고 있다는 것이다. 자유시보는 “민주주의 진영 전체가 경계해야 할 심각한 문제”라며 “이러한 침투가 이미 민주주의 국가의 문턱까지 도달했음을 보여준다”고 주장했다. 한편 미국 시엔엔(CNN) 등은 지난 12일 토드 블랜치 미국 법무장관이 앨리스 황의 간첩 의혹에 대해서 조사하고 있으나 결론을 내리지 못했다고 말했다고 보도했다. 시엔엔은 소식통들을 인용해 미국 국가정보국(DNI)이 앨리스 황을 중국 간첩으로 규정하는 것을 정확하지 않고 과장된 측면이 있다고 보고 있다고 전했다. 미국 중앙정보국(CIA) 관계자들도 확보된 정보만으로 앨리스 황이 중국에 고의로 정보를 넘겼다고 보기는 어렵다고 판단했다고 시엔엔은 전했다. 조해영 기자 hycho@hani.co.kr

articles.title: Huang Resignation Destabilizes Opaque Cross-Strait Semiconductor Backchannels
articles.content: China Brief A weekly digest of the stories you should be following in China, plus exclusive analysis. Delivered Tuesday. Palmer-James-foreign-policy-columnist20 James Palmer By James Palmer , a deputy editor at Foreign Policy . U.S. President Donald Trump is shaking hands with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang outside on a paved road outside the White House. They are both wearing dark suits; Huang is smiling. Additional people, including Tesla CEO Elon Musk, stand in the background, with leafy green trees behind them. U.S. President Donald Trump greets then-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang following a meeting with artificial intelligence executives at the White House in Washington on Sept. 29. Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images United States China James Palmer November 13, 2026, 2:50 PM Welcome to Foreign Policy ’s China Brief. Today’s special edition comes in the wake of Jensen Huang’s resignation as CEO of Nvidia over multiple reported affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy. Welcome to Foreign Policy ’s China Brief. Today’s special edition comes in the wake of Jensen Huang’s resignation as CEO of Nvidia over multiple reported affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy. Huang Resigns From Nvidia In another world, recently resigned Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s infidelities would be a private embarrassment. In this one, however, a powerful man’s poor judgment could steer the U.S.-China technology relationship onto the rocks. Huang admitted to marital infidelity; he reportedly engaged in affairs with at least three women, including two Nvidia employees. His relationship with Alice Huang, a businesswoman and alleged Chinese asset, has drawn the most scrutiny. But why is the relationship, and his resignation on Thursday, so potentially explosive? Broadly speaking, U.S. policy toward China has long been divided into two camps. The caution camp, exemplified by national security hawks, worries about China’s record of intellectual property theft, its control of critical supply chains, its economic might, and its potential to leapfrog the United States in key technologies such as artificial intelligence. The opportunity camp focuses instead on what the relationship with China could offer: selling technology, tapping vast Chinese markets, and finding ways for cooperation and mutual investment . The tension between the two can produce good policy, especially when each side argues smartly against the other. But this healthy debate depends on good faith, on both sides believing that they share a basic set of U.S. national interests. It depends on caution not curdling into racist paranoia and on opportunity not turning into personal greed. The Nvidia debate is particularly intense because there is no hotter resource in the U.S.-China relationship right now than compute: raw processing power, which depends on advanced chips. Unlike most other domains of U.S.-China competition, such as supply chains or critical minerals, this is the rare case where the United States holds the upper hand: roughly 75 percent of global compute , compared with China’s 15 percent. That edge rests on the U.S. alliance with Taiwan, home to chipmaker TSMC, as well as on companies, such as Nvidia, that design and sell these chips. For years, the argument over how to manage China’s access to advanced chips swayed between caution and opportunity. The opportunists argued that Chinese dependence was a good thing. If China could buy everything but the most advanced chips, it would remain reliant on U.S. firms; if China were cut off, it would build its own industry. But the cautious approach—that Beijing should be kept from buying the most advanced chips, thereby locking in the U.S. advantage—generally prevailed. The deal that Nvidia struck with U.S. President Donald Trump last year blew a hole in all of those arguments and in the assumption of good faith. Nvidia was allowed to sell the extremely advanced H200 chip to China not because it won a reasoned debate but because the White House was offered a cut : 25 percent of the sales revenue, with no apparent oversight of the money. Huang via Nvidia also donated $26 million to pro-Trump causes, including construction of the White House ballroom. The deal was rotten from the start, but national security hawks, fearing retaliation from Trump, were quieter than they might have been otherwise. Now the situation is reversed. An incoming Democratic Congress, backed by those Republicans who still care about national security, is poised to scrutinize these deals relentlessly. The spy allegations against Alice Huang have supercharged that scrutiny, as has the White House’s apparent disregard of earlier warnings about her. If it emerges that Trump profited by shorting Nvidia stock after a second warning, the case becomes far worse. Even if Alice Huang never influenced Jensen Huang’s decisions, it will be easy to portray him as swayed by Beijing. Huang’s downfall lets opponents of chip sales depict companies such as Nvidia as tools of the Chinese state and the White House as their willing accomplice. Trump’s doubling down on support for Huang only hands them more ammunition. With Republicans reeling from the U.S. midterm elections, companies can no longer afford to bet solely on Trump’s protection. In the long run, the scandal might expose a wider circle of corruption and sanctions evasion surrounding the $4 trillion company. Nvidia’s most advanced family of chips, Blackwell, is still banned from export to China, yet signs of its usage are all over Chinese AI, and Chinese firms are working hard to acquire it. Some U.S. national security officials appear to have been waiting for the right moment to leak incriminating documents. Alice Huang’s firm, Megaspeed, somehow jumped from $33 million in assets in 2023 to $3 billion in 2024, which suggests possible Chinese state investment and use as a vehicle for sanctions evasion. (Megaspeed denies any wrongdoing and has promised full cooperation with U.S. criminal investigations.) The United States had already started prosecuting companies believed to be evading sanctions, but a full federal investigation into both Jensen Huang’s and Alice Huang’s activities could turn over many more stones. China, as usual, denies any involvement in espionage and urges the United States not to impose new tech restrictions . But those restrictions, and much tighter scrutiny of deals involving chips or China, now look inevitable. Hopefully, Beijing will accept that as part of the game and not retaliate by tightening its own already extensive anti-sanctions regulations or cutting off U.S. supplies of critical minerals. On the U.S. side, there is also a risk of overindexing on a single case—a recurrent habit of intelligence services. The recruitment of one young American by the Chinese intelligence services in the early 2000s, for instance, made the security clearance process far harder for every U.S. citizen who had worked or studied in China. At worst, that overindexing could mean racial bias against anyone of Chinese descent working in sensitive technology in the United States. At the very least, it should make any U.S. businessperson more cautious about dealing with their Chinese counterparts, let alone sleeping with them—and perhaps that is for the better. articles.content: Insider Your all-access pass to FP By Cameron Abadi , a deputy editor at Foreign Policy , and Adam Tooze , a columnist at Foreign Policy and director of the European Institute at Columbia University. Sign up for Adam’s Chartbook newsletter here . Huang, a man in a dark leather jacket, gestures with one hand as he stands beside a large, illuminated electronic server component displayed against a dark background. To hear this entire conversation, and more episodes in the weeks ahead, follow Ones and Tooze wherever you get your podcasts. The semiconductor manufacturer Nvidia, which had until recently been the most valuable company in the world, was thrown into turmoil this past week. Company founder and CEO Jensen Huang resigned upon allegations that he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy and subsequently intervened to sell Nvidia chips to her China-tied company, despite U.S. regulations in place to prevent China’s access to the technology. The scandal has put a spotlight on the widespread international practice of economic espionage—and also on the Trump administration’s susceptibility to corruption. What is the difference between industrial espionage and economic espionage? Is the tech elite particularly vulnerable to this type of spying? And will China be successful at incorporating any AI technologies that it managed to steal? The semiconductor manufacturer Nvidia, which had until recently been the most valuable company in the world, was thrown into turmoil this past week. Company founder and CEO Jensen Huang resigned upon allegations that he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy and subsequently intervened to sell Nvidia chips to her China-tied company, despite U.S. regulations in place to prevent China’s access to the technology. The scandal has put a spotlight on the widespread international practice of economic espionage—and also on the Trump administration’s susceptibility to corruption. What is the difference between industrial espionage and economic espionage? Is the tech elite particularly vulnerable to this type of spying? And will China be successful at incorporating any AI technologies that it managed to steal? Those are just a few of the questions that came up in my recent conversation with FP economics columnist Adam Tooze on the podcast we co-host, Ones and Tooze . What follows is an excerpt, edited for length and clarity. For the full conversation, look for Ones and Tooze wherever you get your podcasts. And check out Adam’s Substack newsletter. Cameron Abadi: What are the differences exactly between industrial espionage, economic intelligence, and economic espionage? Adam Tooze: In general understanding, industrial espionage is above all targeted at particular businesses by, more often than not, other businesses but sometimes by governments. And it’s about accessing commercial secrets, business secrets, business strategies, business technologies. And it involves various types of subterfuge or illegal action. Economic espionage is sort of blurred into that zone, because it also involves various types of subterfuge. But when we say economic espionage, one immediately thinks of governments. Why is that? I think because when we think of businesses, we think of private economic activity and profit. But when we use the word “economy,” we immediately start thinking about GDP and national interest. And so, the sorts of information that are being targeted there might be more to do with technologies of general strategic interest. So that will be different from industrial espionage or purely commercial espionage. And then an example of economic intelligence would be, say, wartime efforts on the part of the British who are aiming a strategic bombing program against Germany and therefore need to understand how the German economy functions and built an economics intelligence wing of the British military war effort so as to organize that. And that ranged from people who were architectural historians who knew which cities would be inflammable if you dropped incendiary bombs on them all the way through to an understanding of the input-output diagram, the supply chains. And it involves, more often than not, open-source information. It doesn’t involve any subterfuge at all. And so economic intelligence kind of blurs into the world that we’re in, of economic reporting, of newsletters, of regular updates. The Economist magazine has what it used to call the Economist Intelligence Unit, which was presumably very well-connected journalists doing studies. And I think the allegation in the Nvidia case sits most squarely in the domain of economic espionage. Yes, it targets a particular business and the top man in that particular business, the charismatic figurehead, indeed, of the entire hardware side of AI. So it would seem that it sits somewhere on that boundary. I don’t think the allegation, however, is that Jensen Huang’s lover was doing this with a view to commercially profiting herself. I think the suggestion is that it’s MSS, the Ministry of State Security, which is doing this on behalf of the Chinese state . CA: Jensen Huang is said to have fallen prey to a honey-trap method of espionage, in which a spy creates a sexual relationship to later exploit it. Is our current economic elite in tech companies particularly susceptible to this form of espionage? AT: It’s impossible not to speculate about the ego makeup of Silicon Valley engineers. It wouldn’t, after all, be surprising if there was a desire for compensation for a whole variety of inhibitions, which no doubt are introduced at various stages in many people’s careers during their extraordinary efforts in very recondite zones of technical expertise. So, the nerd gone wild at the head of a company, the loneliness of people in that kind of position, all of this, I think, no doubt plays a role. But then I was thinking, actually sociologically, and I came to this strange realization, because I spend quite a lot of time in hotels because of this weird existence that I have. And I was thinking to myself, if a senior soldier goes to a hotel, on the face of it, you’re kind of wondering what the senior soldier is doing in a hotel, right? If a senior civil servant, pretty much whichever government they work for, goes to a really glamorous hotel, again, you’d be asking yourself, how can they afford that? That’s not really where they belong, right? So suddenly, you realize that the whole zone of high-end, expensive, relatively exclusive hospitality that presumably provides the most attractive zone for this kind of entrapment, the actors for whom it arouses zero legitimacy issues, zero need for explanation at all, in fact it’s completely normal and taken for granted, are high-level business figures. In fact, the entire conference circuit, where people stay, the blending in those spaces of leisure and business activity, including pools and gyms and eating and drinking as a matter of course, in fact, isa kind of mandate for many businesses. I’ve gone to a lot of these investor conferences, and it’s quite clear that networking is an absolutely required option, right? There’s no excuse for just withdrawing to your room and getting on with your life, which I’d want to do most of the time. And so presumably, this is precisely the world in which this works. I mean, business people systematically expect to be wined and dined. They expect to be courted. They constantly struggle to draw the line between reasonable inducements and bribery. That is an essential part of their business. And many of them, of course, have very strict codes of ethics. But it’s a matter of record that those shift all the time. And they’re much more like, in that sense, the Chinese Communist Party than they are like, you know, conventional civil service jobs in the West, where it’s just quite clear that accepting any kind of gift in any form is just off-limits. No one in the civil service is regularly invited to glamorous parties where there’s a mixture of more or less formally clad, in some cases scantily clad, different types of interaction. And so it’s a kind of recipe for stress on this fault line, I would have thought. And it’s purely sociological, it’s not a matter of psychology at all. CA: There’s clearly a distinction between pursuing the acquisition of technologies through espionage of this kind versus productively absorbing that technology upon having acquired it. How does that distinction apply right now to China? AT: I think this is the whole game, actually. The real reason to be worried is that China has a demonstrated and extraordinary capacity to incorporate. In other words, it’s a near-peer . And that’s precisely what makes it so alarming to Western security officials, is that there’s absolutely every reason to think they can, yeah. And furthermore, leapfrog, even . Give them half a chance and there’s every single reason to think that they can generalize it, make it cheaper, speed it up. There are differences, obviously, because what Nvidia does or what Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company does or what the lithograph makers do is literally special source. Like, no one has ever done that anywhere, ever, in the entire world in the history of humanity. So whether you can replicate that is an open question. But that’s presumably what the Chinese aren’t going to do anyway. They’re going to make their own version that’s more suitable to their circumstances. And it’s critical to know—and we don’t know what’s actually happened in this case—but there are certain critical problems that it’s interesting to know how other people solve them, because it helps you to think about how you should solve them in your own terms. And that is why I think the Chinese case is so significant, because they have a demonstrated capacity to do that. And it really varies—in regard to transport engineering, cars, railways, solar, batteries, there has already been hugely successful leapfrogging; the game is over. With regard to chips, it’s a slightly different story, and I think that speaks to the fact that the technological demands are just so mind-blowingly high . But that does contrast very significantly with the Soviet Union, which at different periods in its history demonstrated greater- and lesser-degree capacity to incorporate technologies that it acquired through espionage. So around the atomic bomb program, there was a quite a high capacity to incorporate. Then of course in rocketry, they become world-leading. And they do that like the Americans by capturing German rocket scientists and then incorporating their knowledge into what was already a high-functioning military industrial system in the Soviet Union that was wasteful of people’s lives but was generative of a whole series of incredibly innovative, very, very powerful and effective weapons. But more generally, it’s a remarkable instance of just how little can get transferred, because after all, the Soviet Union was the beneficiary, after ‘45, of a huge wave—this is the untold story of German reparations after World War II, absolutely gigantic, and they take the form principally of dismantling. So vast amounts of German equipment are shipped to the Soviet Union where, I don’t think it’s merely apocryphal to say, an awful lot of it just rusted and was not fully incorporated into the Soviet system. Now, in earlier stages, they had done much better. So in the ‘30s, the Stalinist industrialization program is heavily dependent on American expertise and on German expertise funded in part by export guarantees from the Weimar Republic that helped to fund this flow. So it wasn’t consistently rubbish at incorporating, but it certainly wasn’t the powerhouse of creative imitation, adaptation, modification, and improvement that China is, to an extent that nowhere else in the world can match, right? That’s the extraordinary thing. They can iterate, they can modify, they could incorporate at a pace that no one else in the world—in almost all areas of production—no one else can match. And so, then if you feed that with privileged insider information, then you’d expect really large-scale effects. articles.title: Delta Chief Blames Decades of FAA Underfunding for Air Gridlock
articles.content: Last year, chronic flight delays and cancellations at Newark Liberty International Airport revealed a litany of problems with antiquated air traffic control systems. Today, those problems persist and are even more illuminated thanks to the FAA’s nationwide ground stop on Friday. Recommended Video Even Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy admitted last year that some of the decades-old computer equipment air traffic controllers use looks like it came off the set of Apollo 13 , and compared it to a 1967 Volkswagen Beetle. Delta CEO Ed Bastian also revealed last year that, due to aging air traffic control systems, it actually takes longer today to fly from Atlanta to LaGuardia than it did in the 1950s when the airline opened that route. “That’s the air traffic control system. It’s very slow. It’s congested,” he told TODAY in May 2025. “If you modernize the skies, you can kind of bring greater efficiency.” By modernizing the skies, the airline chief means using satellite technology, the latest state-of-the-art equipment, and GPS. But currently, air traffic controllers have to use a radar point-and-shoot system from the 1960s. “The screens look like something out of the 1960s and ‘70s,” Bastian said. “Our controllers and our operators need the best in order to keep us safe and make sure it maintains its safety record.” Despite a barrage of emergency landings, machinery failure, a collision, and other air traffic control failures in the airline industry reported this year, he insists it’s still safe to fly. “It is absolutely safe. It’s the safest form of transportation in the world,” Bastian said. “The most skilled aviation professionals in the world work and operate the U.S. airspace. So it is absolutely safe.” But just because it’s safe doesn’t mean it’s acceptable for the U.S. to have such antiquated technology operating its airspace, Bastian said. Although there is bipartisan support to modernize America’s air traffic control system, it’s a process that requires a lot of time and money. On May 8, 2025, Duffy and President Donald Trump announced a plan to build a brand-new air traffic control system “that will be the envy of the world.” The plan includes replacing outdated infrastructure with wireless and satellite technologies at more than 4,600 air traffic control sites, building six new air traffic coordination centers, and replacing towers and terminal radar approach control (TRACONs). “Our antiquated air traffic control system is affecting our workforce,” the Federal Aviation Administration said in a statement. “As Secretary Duffy has said, we must get the best safety technology in the hands of controllers as soon as possible.” Reuters reported in late March the FAA was short about 3,500 air traffic controllers. On Friday, Duffy called on Congress to appropriate $50 billion for modernization. The House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, though, estimates it could cost $12.5 billion . The Modern Skies Coalition , an umbrella group for aviation industry groups, estimated it would cost $31 billion or more. But in the short term, the airline industry is making adjustments to improve flight delays and cancellations that result from air traffic control problems. Many airlines are pulling down their operations at Newark, Bastian said, which reduces some of the congestion at the airport. “Now, that’s not good in the long run. It’s not good for consumers,” Bastian said. “It’s not good for the airport itself, but it’s the only thing that we have in the meantime.” A version of this story originally published on Fortune.com on May 16, 2025. articles.title: Activist Shareholders Pressure Nvidia Board for Jensen Huang Restoration
articles.content: LivestreamMenuAltimeter Capital’s Brad Gerstner and Atreides Management’s Gavin Baker asked Nvidia’s board to conduct a slow, deliberate CEO search that leaves open the possibility of Jensen Huang’s return.The firms disclosed about $2.13 billion of Nvidia stock combined as of June 30.Huang resigned as president, CEO and director on Nov. 12 after reports about personal relationships and amid an independent board investigation; Nvidia’s resignation announcement did not state a reason.In this article Two major Nvidia shareholders are calling on the board of directors to weigh all options for the company's future leadership, including "the potential return of Jensen Huang." Altimeter Capital CEO Brad Gerstner posted a letter on X on Friday that urges Nvidia's board to "pursue a slow, measured, and deliberate process regarding the future leadership of Nvidia." The letter is also signed by Atreides Management's Gavin Baker. Nvidia was Altimeter Capital's largest disclosed equity holding in its most recent SEC filing, with a 9.4 million-share stake worth nearly $1.9 billion as of June 30. Atreides held 1.2 million shares worth nearly $250 million at the end of June. The letter said Nvidia will be "capably led" by interim CEO Colette Kress, who served as Nvidia's CFO for 13 years before the board announced Thursday that she'd lead the company in Huang's absence. "But the Founder and long time incredible leader of this extraordinary company has earned the right for a deliberate process that avoids any needless rush to replace him before all the facts are known," the letter concludes. The document did not call for Huang's immediate reinstatement. Nvidia founder Jensen Huang resigned on Thursday amid multiple affair allegations, including one with suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang, who also worked with Nvidia customer Megaspeed. The Singapore-based company is being investigated by the Justice Department for possibly redirecting some of its supply of Nvidia's restricted artificial intelligence chips to China. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said on X Friday that he signed a petition asking to reinstate Huang. A petition circulating online called "Stand with Jensen" claims to have more than 100,000 signatures, including more than 5,000 current Nvidia employees. Musk said on X Saturday that without Huang, some "critical deals will be lost." Another letter sent Friday called on U.S. Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick to testify about Megaspeed before the House Intelligence Committee. Lutnick has agreed to testify before the Senate Banking Committee on Dec. 10 about whether the Commerce Department is "properly performing its broader role of preventing China from acquiring advanced AI chips," according to the letter. Huang has also been asked to testify. The Commerce Department originally launched an investigation into Megaspeed that was moved to the Justice Department in 2025 after Nvidia's lawyer contacted a senior Commerce official, according to The New York Times. President Donald Trump is scheduled to visit China on Thursday, but doesn't plan to raise Nvidia and the suspected spy affair during his meeting with Chinese president Xi Jinping, according to U.S. officials. Musk is expected to join Trump on the trip to Shenzhen, China, for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit on Nov. 18 and 19.

articles.title: Anthropic Massive Capex Demands Strain Sovereign AI Investor Reserves
articles.content: Advertisement SKIP ADVERTISEMENT Dario Amodei, Anthropic’s chief executive, introduced his artificial intelligence company to potential stock market investors this week with a sublime vision. He predicted the end of cancer and mental illness within a decade, and a transformation of cognitive work. “If we do this right, we can create an age of miracles,” he said in a marketing video for Anthropic’s initial public offering. Wall Street is grappling with how much it may cost to get to utopia. Stock analysts at Goldman Sachs, the investment bank leading Anthropic’s I.P.O., have told investors privately this week that they forecast the company will burn through more than $65 billion next year, and another $41 billion in 2028, said two people familiar with those discussions. Those totals would make Anthropic’s spending among the most aggressive corporate bets on funding the giant A.I. infrastructure build-out. “We are in aggressive investment mode,” Krishna Rao, Anthropic’s chief financial officer, said in the video, without discussing specific spending forecasts. That spending would create a drastically different financial picture than Anthropic has shown recently. The company generated cash from its business in the first nine months of this year, its I.P.O. prospectus shows, a feat in the expensive business of A.I. model development. It has barely spent the $141 billion it raised privately from investors. The listing on Nasdaq, expected next Thursday, could value Anthropic at $1.4 trillion. It would not only cement its status as one of the world’s most prominent companies but hand it additional firepower to help it pull further ahead of well-heeled rivals like OpenAI and Alphabet. The I.P.O. would deliver Anthropic an additional $100 billion to spend, and make it easier to raise even more money to fund those huge commitments. But Anthropic’s public debut will lead to costs that don’t appear today. It said in the prospectus it anticipated about $40 billion of expenses in the coming years tied to preexisting stock grants it has given employees that haven’t yet hit its accounting books. The company’s investor prospectus pegged the size of the future bill that Anthropic has run up for chips, power and other computing infrastructure to help it develop more advanced A.I. models at $900 billion over the next two decades. Stock pickers and analysts said the prospectus is missing more granular details about the spending, like how much is going toward A.I. training and research, serving customers and the company’s own internal uses of its A.I. service Claude. “There’s definitely a desire to keep the focus on the massive, broad huge opportunity ahead of us, rather than go into the specifics,” said Ashley MacNeill, managing director at the private equity firm Vista Equity Partners. Ms. MacNeill, a former investment banker who worked on high-profile tech I.P.O.s, added that she didn’t think Anthropic was “trying to hide the ball” but said the lack of disclosures “creates a vagueness on how they will run this company from a cost perspective going forward.” Investors are bracing for Anthropic to run up the bill regardless. The size of the existing financial commitments the company laid out “is likely going to be meaningfully short of what Anthropic ultimately needs,” analysts at the investment bank William Blair wrote to investors this week. The report characterized Anthropic’s pace of constantly releasing new versions of Claude as a “model treadmill.” The analysts wrote that the company’s potential valuation was attractive but added that “we empathize with investors that call out the risk of a company in a 4-year-old industry.” Part of investors’ challenge is determining exactly what kind of business they’re signing up to support. Anthropic’s ascent has been dizzying. In one year, the company grew quarterly sales from about $1 billion, roughly the size of the dating app Tinder’s parent company Match Group, to $17 billion, the size of more-than-century-old stalwarts like Pfizer and IBM. Anthropic executives have stressed that they have a lot more room to grow. Its focus on corporate customers, rather than consumers, has helped it leapfrog the ChatGPT maker OpenAI in sales this year. Its success has largely been thanks to heavy adoption by software developers. Next, they’re going after a wider range of white-collar employees to automate more of a variety of work tasks. “To most workers, Claude is still just a chatbot,” Nicholas Lin, an Anthropic employee, said in an interview on Monday. The company is trying to change that. On Tuesday, it introduced new tools for people to include Claude as a participant in a work meeting or a spreadsheet. The company will need those products to catch on. Goldman Sachs, in its private forecast to investors, predicted that Anthropic would surpass $440 billion in annual revenue by 2029, more sales than Apple generated last year. That surge would help Anthropic generate enough cash to cover its costs by that year, according to the forecast. The Financial Times earlier reported on the investment bank’s forecast. But Anthropic’s customers aren’t locked into long-term contracts, and the vast majority of the company’s revenue is generated by versions of its A.I. models it released in the last six months, according to the prospectus. Shivaram Rajgopal, a professor of accounting and auditing at Columbia Business School, said that could be a problem if Anthropic can’t gain enough customer loyalty and keep prices high. In a worst-case scenario, the company could have similar business dynamics to Netflix, which has to continue spending heavily on producing shows to keep subscribers. “That’s a business model risk,” Dr. Rajgopal said. “These are slow-moving disasters.” Anthropic, for its part, said the computing bills to develop new A.I. models will pay off. The spending, it argued, creates a reinforcing cycle that will help it keep its lead in the A.I. race, and eventually generate profits. Executives say customers have kept spending on Claude because its new model versions keep getting better, and the company can also keep costs down for customers and itself as models improve. The company considers itself the ultimate beneficiary of its own creation, as it uses Claude to automate and speed up its model development. Anthropic published a report last month that suggested its A.I. agents, or tools that can complete work tasks like writing code or creating spreadsheets, worked six times as many hours in a week as its human employees. “Our pace of discovery is speeding up, and a lot of that acceleration comes from Claude itself,” Sam McCandlish, an Anthropic co-founder and chief architect, said in the investor video. Many investors weighing the deal haven’t seen Claude transform their work in the same way. “There’s an anxiousness and disconnect you see within A.I. believers and nonbelievers,” Ms. MacNeill said. “We’ve only sat with this technology for a few years.” Corrected on Nov. 13, 2026 : An earlier version of this article misstated Ashley MacNeill’s position at the private equity firm Vista Equity Partners. articles.title: Congressional Subpoenas Target Huang Despite Nvidia Exit and Resignation
articles.content: Jensen Huang may be out at Nvidia , but the questions surrounding his relationship with a suspected Chinese spy—and what it might have meant for American national security—are only growing more serious. The billionaire’s resignation Thursday has done little to quiet a scandal that threatens to reach well beyond Nvidia’s boardroom, raising questions about the Trump administration’s controversial decisions to loosen restrictions on AI chip sales to China. Huang played an influential role in shaping those policies. Now, Congress wants to know whether his personal relationship with a Chinese businesswoman exposed sensitive American technology or national security information to Beijing—and what government officials knew about the potential risks. Despite his departure as Nvidia’s chairman and CEO, Huang has reportedly agreed to testify before congressional investigators. The former CEO and lawmakers have been discussing the timing of the closed-door hearing, which could provide answers about his relationship with an executive at a company suspected of funneling restricted Nvidia chips to Chinese AI labs. Three Republican committee chairs in the House of Representatives—Reps. Brian Mast, John Moolenaar, and Rick Crawford—requested Huang’s testimony in a November 4 letter , more than a week before his resignation. Mast told reporters Thursday that his committee still wanted to speak to Huang, adding that his staff had been in contact with Huang’s team as recently as Wednesday night. Later that day, Bloomberg and NBC News reported that Huang had agreed to appear without a subpoena. The request followed an October 29 New York Times investigation into Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed, a company U.S. intelligence had suspected for more than a year of collaborating with the Chinese government and helping funnel trade-restricted AI chips to Chinese labs. The lawmakers are concerned that Alice Huang may also have provided Beijing with access to trade secrets and sensitive national security information. “Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the PRC’s (People’s Republic of China) access to sensitive U.S. technology and information,” the chairmen wrote. “The issue of PRC infiltration and access to cutting-edge U.S. technology is core to the investigative work of our three committees this Congress. It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which U.S. national security has been placed at risk.” But the congressional scrutiny is no longer limited to Huang or Nvidia. Lawmakers are increasingly asking whether the Trump administration overlooked warnings about potential Chinese espionage while allowing the company to expand sales of advanced AI chips to China. On November 11, Democratic Senators Elizabeth Warren and Chris Coons sent a letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller demanding that the administration preserve documents concerning Nvidia’s chip exports, the suspected intelligence operation, and government investigations into Megaspeed. The senators specifically requested records concerning an intelligence memorandum reportedly circulated to senior administration officials ahead of Trump’s May 2026 visit to China. They also sought communications between Huang and Trump, records of discussions about chip export restrictions, and documents concerning the government’s handling of its investigation into Megaspeed. The question, at the core of their inquiry, is whether national security concerns were sidelined as Huang and the Trump administration pursued policies that benefited Nvidia. Huang has been one of the tech industry’s most prominent supporters of Donald Trump. Nvidia contributed $1 million to Trump’s inaugural fund and $25 million toward the White House ballroom now under construction. Huang himself has visited Trump’s Mar-a-Lago resort in Florida and the White House numerous times, and has traveled with the president. His influence on U.S. export policy regarding AI chips is evident. He’s credited with persuading the Trump administration to allow sales of Nvidia H20 and H200 chips to China. Huang argued that letting the chips, and the CUDA software framework that runs them, proliferate around the world was good for America. Nvidia also agreed to pay the U.S. government 15% of revenue from H20 sales and 25% from H200 sales. Nvidia defended the arrangement last December. “The Administration’s licensing process will ensure that sales of H200 to authorized customers worldwide do not deprive U.S. customers of anything—and will in fact benefit American national and economic security,” spokesman John Rizzo said in a statement to Fast Company . “Offering H200 to approved and known commercial customers, vetted by the Department of Commerce, raises no cybersecurity risk and strikes a thoughtful balance that is great for America.” Those assurances now face renewed scrutiny. Megaspeed bought billions of dollars’ worth of Nvidia chips in recent years, including some of its most powerful Blackwell chips, which remain off limits to Chinese labs. A New York Times report last year described finding boxes of powerful Nvidia chips at a nearly empty Megaspeed office in Malaysia, raising suspicions that the company was serving as a conduit for restricted technology bound for China. There are also unanswered questions about the government’s response. The Commerce Department opened an investigation into Megaspeed last year, but the inquiry was subsequently transferred to the Department of Justice, with little publicly known about what happened afterward. The Warren–Coons letter seeks records that could help establish what senior Trump administration officials knew about the suspected Chinese intelligence operation, why the White House and the Commerce Department allowed chip shipments to Megaspeed to continue, and whether or not the White House disregarded national security recommendations to accommodate Nvidia’s commercial interests. These questions could become more consequential when Democrats take control of Congress in January. Coons, who is expected to chair the powerful Senate Foreign Relations Committee, has also called for an investigation into Huang and Nvidia to determine whether national security was compromised while Nvidia and the White House benefited financially from chip sales to China. “We need answers about the relationship between AI billionaires and the Trump administration,” Coons wrote on X . I’m pushing to investigate Jensen Huang and Nvidia to determine whether our national security was compromised. We need answers about the relationship between AI billionaires and the Trump administration, who's making these decisions, and who's really got their hand on the wheel. — Senator Chris Coons (@ChrisCoons) November 9, 2026 For Nvidia, meanwhile, the immediate consequences have been severe. Its shares have lost nearly a quarter of their value—24.6%—since The New York Times first reported on Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang on October 29. Nvidia has not publicly offered a detailed explanation for accepting Huang’s resignation. Its SEC filing simply states that the board accepted his departure. But the decision may have had less to do with the morality of Huang’s personal conduct than with the growing financial and political risks of keeping him in charge. articles.title: Nvidia Interim Leadership Imposes Radical Austerity Following Huang Departure
articles.content: Former Nvidia CEO and cofounder Jensen Huang famously avoided unnecessary meetings, prioritizing efficiency over routine check-ins. Even with, at one point, 60 direct reports , he refused to do catch-ups. Now that he’s resigned , the question is whether his successor (currently Colette Kress who has stepped up on an interim basis) will keep the rule. Recommended Video Speaking at Stanford University , Huang once disclosed his aversion to frequent catch-ups. “I don’t do one-on-ones with any of them,” he said. Huang argued frequent meetings would clutter his schedule. He said they would also get in the way of the broader team’s ability to address challenges, work effectively, and stay transparent. “They never hear me say something to them, that is only for them to know,” he said. “There’s not one piece of information that I somehow secretly tell the staff; I don’t tell the rest of the company.” “In that way, our company was designed for agility. For information to be to flow as quickly as possible. For people to be empowered by what they are able to do, not what they know,” he added. But that doesn’t mean he had no time for his team. Huang insisted he still regularly caught up with his executives. They just didn’t need to set time aside in their diaries to be on the same page. “I write no reviews for any of them,” he added. “I give them constant reviews and they provide the same to me.” And when an employee genuinely needed a moment of his time, Huang insisted he’d “drop everything for them.” Stepping into Huang’s shoes (for now) is CFO Colette Kress . The interim CEO, who has an estimated net worth of $1.2 billion according to Forbes , holds a bachelor’s in finance from the University of Arizona and an MBA from Southern Methodist University. After nearly three decades’ worth of financial roles at companies such as Texas Instruments , Cisco, and Microsoft , she joined Nvidia in September 2013. Since then, she guided the company’s finances through a significant transformation, from a business largely focused on video game hardware to a chipmaking powerhouse at the center of the AI boom—and watched its market cap soar from about $9 billion to, at its peak, $5 trillion. Its since dropped below $4 trillion upon the news regarding Huang. She hasn’t revealed whether she’ll ditch one-on-ones too. But the 59-year-old, who has spent 13 years as Huang’s right hand on Nvidia’s finances, seems to share his affinity for efficiency. “We do not waste a day, we don’t waste a dime,” Kress said in 2024. “And those two things are really important about us, our agility to move fast, but our ability to not waste things along the way.” Huang isn’t the first leader to argue that meetings aren’t the best use of time. Pandora’s former CEO Alexander Lacik told Fortune too many meetings result in every department or company issue getting “equal attention”—whether or not it needs it. He limited his catch-ups with management. “There’s only one, two, three activities that actually draw disproportionate value and the rest is just background noise,” he said. “As time has gone by and I’m getting towards the end of my career, I’m much more clear on trying to insert myself where I make a high impact.” United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby caps his meetings at four hours a day , and wants the ones he does attend to be “quick” and “almost all conversational.” E-commerce giant Shopify took one step further and actually axed all meetings involving more than two people in 2023, in a company-wide “calendar purge” meant to give employees more time to work on other tasks. And even Amazon founder Jeff Bezos—a big fan of “ messy meetings ”—mandates a strict protocol to ensure they’re actually useful, complete with a six-page memo instead of a PowerPoint (because they’re too vague) and half an hour set aside at the start of the meeting to silently read it together before having “a really elevated discussion.” A version of this story was published on Fortune.com on June 12, 2024. articles.content: A planned logistics cluster in the Hung Shui Kiu/Ha Tsuen development area in Hong Kong’s Northern Metropolis has received 16 expression-of-interest submissions, the government has said. This aerial photo shows the demolition of Yik Yuen Tsuen, a village near the future Hung Shui Kiu MTR station, October 30, 2026. On the top right corner of the photo shows a large area planned for the campus area of the Hung Shui Kiu University Town. Photo: Kyle Lam/HKFP. Authorities announced on Friday that the 16 submissions came from developers, logistics operators, industry associations and professional services providers, without naming them. They were signalling interest in a roughly 32-hectare land plot in the Hung Shui Kiu/Ha Tsuen New Development Area that authorities have reserved for building a “modern logistics cluster” in the western part of the Northern Metropolis. The Transport and Logistics Bureau (TLB) and the Civil Engineering and Development Department oversee this part of the project. A TLB spokesperson said authorities would start analysing the submissions to facilitate planning and the preparation of a formal tender. “We expect to invite tenders for the first available site(s) in end [of] 2027 at the earliest, with a view to awarding the relevant tender in 2028,” the spokesperson added. The Hung Shui Kiu/Ha Tsuen logistics cluster will be close to the Shenzhen Bay Port and connected to the Hong Kong International Airport and the Kwai Tsing Container Terminals, the government has said. Lawmakers on Thursday passed dedicated legislation that will streamline regulatory procedures and expedite the Northern Metropolis development, which is set to transform about a third of Hong Kong’s land area near its border with Shenzhen into an innovation and tech hub. articles.title: Regulatory Hurdles and Collapsing Demand Derail Tesla Cybertruck Ambitions
articles.content: Medio volgend jaar loopt in Tesla’s Gigafactory in Texas volgens plan de laatste Cybertruck van de band. Het monster was pas drie jaar in de handel. Teslabaas Elon Musk wil naar eigen zeggen productiefaciliteiten vrijmaken voor zijn autonome deelauto, de Cybercab, maar belangrijker is dat de Cybertruck gigantisch flopte. In Europa was hij niet te koop, en in de VS verkocht hij maar mondjesmaat sinds de lancering in 2023, vier jaar nadat hij bij de officiële onthulling van het prototype met een combinatie van hilariteit, bewondering en weerzin was ontvangen. Er zijn ruim 70.000 Cybertrucks gebouwd, terwijl Musk had gehoopt er 250.000 per jaar te kunnen leveren. De Cybertruck was ook wel een buitensporig vreemde vogel; een elektrische reuzen-pick-up van ongelakt roestvrij staal met een elektrisch rolluik om de laadbak af te sluiten. Het puntdak van de cabine deed denken aan de wegdelen van een oud-Hollandse ophaalbrug. De andere associatie, met oude sciencefictionfilms, is geen toeval. De beeldwereld van Ridley Scotts film Blade Runner diende als inspiratiebron. Musk wilde een futuristisch apparaat, een toekomst die eruitzag als de toekomst. De Cybertruck moest een onoverwinnelijke machine worden, onverslaanbaar op de weg én in de modder, bestand tegen alles, superheld op wielen. Dus kwam het niet gelegen dat Tesla-ontwerper Franz von Holzhausen in 2019 live op een podium de zogenaamd onbreekbare pantserruiten met een kogel toch aan diggelen wist te slaan. Bij een tweede poging in 2023 ging het wel goed, maar toen hing er al een damp van tragikomische bluf om de auto. Hier kwam de Cybertruck om veiligheidsredenen het land niet in. De toezichthouder RDW gaf nooit groen licht voor een koets met zulke scherpe, voetgangersvijandige punten en hoeken. Een met mens en have volgeladen Cybertruck had met een leeggewicht van ruim drie ton trouwens alleen met groot-rijbewijs bereden mogen worden. Hij was 5,68 meter lang en met een breedte van 2,20 meter ongeschikt voor alle parkeergarages, ook Amerikaanse. Zoiets bizars was in de autowereld niet vertoond sinds de Hummer H1 en de LM002, in 1986 Lamborghini’s visie op een grote terreinwagen. Maar Musk had weer iets unieks. Voor zolang het duurde. In drie jaar stortte het grote toekomstvisioen als een kaartenhuis in elkaar. Europese media berichtten sinds Musks verbond met Trump niet zonder leedvermaak over technische mankementen en de tegenvallende verkoop. Voor inzittenden en omstanders riskante problemen met vastzittende stroompedalen en losrakende carrosseriepanelen deden de auto geen goed. De tijd waarin idealistische Tesla-klanten die gebreken als onvermijdelijke kinderziekten accepteerden, was voorbij. De verkoopstatistieken anticipeerden op een doodvonnis. In 2025 werden in de VS 28.292 Cybertrucks geregistreerd tegen 828.832 exemplaren voor Fords populaire F-serie, in de VS de bestverkopende pick-up. Ja, de Cybertruck was een machofantasie. Toch was hij op papier een excellent idee voor Tesla’s thuismarkt, de VS. Amerikanen rijden pick-uptrucks, hoe groter hoe beter. De truck is daar wat de steelgitaar voor de country en de rodeostier voor cowboys is, een culturele hoeksteen met in dit geval het bijpassende reactionaire imago. Zo’n conservatieve markt elektrificeren leek een uitdagende, zo niet onmogelijke opdracht, maar Musk had in eerste aanleg het tij mee. Toen hij in het techlandschap nog die politiek onbesmette disruptieve kracht was, stapten hoogopgeleide Democraten blind in een Model S, Y of X, zichtbaar verguld met hun pioniersrol van early adopters . Wat aan Tesla’s van de eerste jaren ook niet deugde, de klanten vergaven Musk alles. Tesla’s van de eerste jaren waren woke on steroids , een speels activistisch ‘nee’ tegen olieboeren en fossiele fabrikanten. De gekke technerd Musk paste nog helemaal in het politiek-correcte plaatje van een duurzame tegencultuur. Een Cybertruck rijdt in Northbrook, een voorstad van Chicago, langs een wereldwijde protestdag tegen Elon Musk en Tesla, vorig jaar maart. Foto ANP Zoom in In dat klimaat had zelfs een Cybertruck kunnen gedijen. Maar toen hij kwam was én Musks imago sterk veranderd, én dat grote ding onwennig nieuw terrein voor een merk dat zijn geboorteweeën net achter de rug had. Een pick-up koop je voor het platteland, waar in de bak een dode koe moet passen. Op de vraag of hillbillies (een geuzennaam van Schots-Ierse Amerikanen uit de Appalachen) met hun zes- en achtcilinder pick-ups van Ford, Dodge en Chevrolet op zo’n ontwerp zaten te wachten, kwam een helder antwoord: niet. Zij die de truck van hun nieuwbakken Trump-maat Musk hadden moeten kopen, bleven hun oude Fords en Chevy’s trouw. Die konden ze bij elke kruising tanken in een land waar de benzine nog altijd grofweg 50 procent goedkoper is dan hier. Alleen in grote steden als Los Angeles en San Francisco werd de Cybertruck een cultauto voor modieuze westcoasttypes. Op het platteland bestond hij niet. Concurrerende elektrische pick-ups van het Amerikaanse Rivian en Ford werden trouwens evenmin succesvol. Amerika bleek niet rijp voor het concept. De Cybertruck was een sociologische scheefwoner, bedoeld voor een publiek dat hem niet eens in overweging nam Voor de gewone pick-upkoper was de Cybertruck ook buitensporig duur. Voor het topmodel, de Cyberbeast, vroeg Tesla ruim een ton in dollars. In de VS koop je voor minder dan de helft zo’n populaire Ford-pick-up met een daar nog voor iedereen aanvaardbare benzinemotor. De Cybertruck was een sociologische scheefwoner, bedoeld voor een publiek dat hem niet eens in overweging nam. Hij was een megalomane brug te ver, maar in de designgeschiedenis zal de Cybertruck een mijlpaal blijven. Geen fabrikant had zoiets op de markt durven brengen. Voor een hoge afschrijving hoeven de laatste kopers niet te vrezen. Met zo’n geringe oplage kan het punthoofd een gezocht collector’s item worden. articles.title: Decaying Federal Telecommunications Trigger Systemic National Flight Suspension
articles.content: Stay Connected Featured eBooks Health Technology: Relaunch of VA EHR Read Now Law Enforcement Technology Read Now Insights & Reports By Frank Konkel , Editor-in-Chief | November 13, 2026 10:17 PM ET The ground stop delayed more than 10,000 flights Friday, though officials said there was no indication of a cyber-attack or relation to the Microsoft outage earlier in the week. FAA The Federal Aviation Administration issued a nationwide ground stop for more than four hours across all U.S. airports Friday, citing “extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety,” impacting at least 10,000 flights and disrupting air travel for more than 2 million passengers. The ground stop was lifted around 9 p.m. EST, after which Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed the ground stop on outdated legacy IT systems in a briefing at the White House. “This is a legacy system problem that took place tonight, and we have to handle it accordingly,” said Duffy, who himself was on a flight back to Washington, D.C. from Dallas after speaking with college students at Texas Christian University when the FAA began experiencing instabilities in radar and communications. “Our switches, our routers, actually got overloaded with data, and they went down,” Duffy explained. “And I shouldn't say they went down. They started to give us inconsistency in the data from those routers. And because of that, we shut the system down." Those inconsistencies resulted in intermittent communication and radar, meaning there were times air traffic controllers could not immediately communicate with pilots or see where aircraft were at. Mullin said the ground stop was issued “out of an abundance of caution,” and said no flights or lives were at risk. He added the ground stop was issued “out of an abundance of caution” after the FAA installed patches and new technology, “overwhelming the older system." Mullin said the National Security Agency, Defense Department, Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, FEMA and other agencies worked together Friday to investigate and address the issues. He said “it does not appear” the issues leading to the ground stop were caused by a cyberattack, and said there was no evidence or “footprints” of anyone improperly accessing or hacking FAA systems. “However, we’re still looking, so we’re not going to rule that out,” he said, after unequivocally stating that the FAA’s issues were not related to recent global Microsoft outages. Duffy said FAA would prioritize larger flights into the weekend and expected delays to compound for several days, but anticipated flight schedules to get back on track before the Thanksgiving rush. During the press briefing, he called on Congress to pass an emergency funding bill that would give the Transportation Department another $50 billion to modernize the nation’s air traffic control system. In 2025, Congress appropriated $12.5 billion through the One Big Beautiful Bill Act to begin that modernization effort , but Duffy said it isn’t enough. He added that new artificial intelligence-powered systems rolled out in recent weeks had nothing to do with the ground stop, and said systems recently upgraded from analog to digital “did not experience these issues.” "It's important that we're able to finish this work with additional resources,” Duffy said. “I got 12 and a half billion, and with that money, we are spending it and spending it well, but the Congress at the time knew that that was not going to be enough,” Duffy said. I think there's no better time than the present to actually give us the money and let us finish the bill. What went down was old, right? It was … old legacy equipment. It failed, and listen, it's going to continue to fail.” Who is to blame? Duffy, during a press conference Saturday, said a technical issue may have arisen during work performed on telecommunications lines by Florida-based defense contractor L3Harris. "At least one of our remote FAA locations, a contractor was doing routine maintenance to switch telecommunication lines from old copper wire, and they were bringing it over to fiber,” Duffy explained. “That contractor that does the work for us is L3Harris. They're a legacy provider. They've been working for the FAA for over 20 years. The network that we use at the FAA to control the airspace — L3Harris actually owns that network.” Duffy further said L3Harris was transitioning the system from analog copper wire to a digital fiber-optic cables when an FAA router on location was apparently flooded with data, quickly impacting additional routers across numerous FAA systems across the country. Duffy said the Transportation Department and FAA are working to assess who — or what — is ultimately responsible for issue. "What we're working to determine was whether we had incompetence — meaning was it user error or installation error from L3Harris — or did they install a faulty router? We haven't determined what the fault was. Was it the router? Or were they not doing great work for us at L3Harris," Duffy said. In a statement, an L3Harris spokesperson said the company “is supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. 13 ground stop of our nation’s air travel.” “L3Harris has been modernizing the communications infrastructure supporting the National Airspace System in close coordination with the FAA. With safety and reliability as our highest priorities, L3Harris, together with its telco partners and the FAA, has completed more than 70% of the planned airspace communications conversion from legacy copper wires to a fiber optic system,” an L3Harris spokesperson said. “L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously.” Editor's note: This story was updated Saturday to include new information. articles.title: Massive Entertainment Releases Stress Corporate Productivity and Network Bandwidth
articles.content: LivestreamMenu"Grand Theft Auto VI" launches Nov. 19, with third-party estimates pointing to exceptional preorder demand and Wall Street expecting tens of millions of copies sold by March.Creators, streaming platforms, food delivery services and Miami tourism could all feel the impact or see spending shift with the game's launch.The game could pull holiday attention from streaming and movies in the week before Thanksgiving.In this article It's been 13 years since the last installment of Grand Theft Auto, and fans are getting ready for what analysts say could be the biggest video game launch of all time. The latest game in the franchise, "Grand Theft Auto VI," is set to launch on Nov. 19, after Take-Two Interactive's Rockstar Games delayed its launch twice. Roth analyst Eric Handler estimated the game maker spent more than $1 billion developing the game. Sales figures could end up breaking records. Sensor Tower estimated over 12 million preorders through Nov. 13, and Morgan Stanley forecast the game could sell 40 million copies by March 2027. Beyond launch week, the Grand Theft Auto, or GTA, franchise has a track record of lasting engagement over many years. Even 13 years after launch, "Grand Theft Auto V" is one of the top five most viewed games on Twitch this year. In anticipation of the game's launch, investors have been taking note: Take-two's stock has more than doubled since the beginning of 2023. The release is seen as not only a monumental moment for developer Rockstar Games and parent company Take-Two, but also a massive opportunity for the entire gaming industry. Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick addressed demand in a recent "Squawk Box" interview, saying, "We tend to be pretty judicious when we talk about this sort of thing, but our expectations were high and they are being vastly exceeded so far." Streamers and creators across the digital ecosystem are looking at the launch as a massive opportunity to drive engagement with their content and fuel subscriber and ad revenue growth. A creator who goes by the name Deansocool, who has 375,000 followers on Twitch and posts content to YouTube and other social platforms as well, said "GTA VI" will enable creators to grow their audience and provide a massive opportunity for newer streamers to make a name for themselves. "This game is going to make a lot of millionaires in 2027. A lot of creators gotta understand this is it. This is that golden ticket. This is like a hundred times bigger than Fortnite," he said in an interview with CNBC. "It goes beyond this launch moment into this sustaining opportunity for them to grow, build, engage and retain their audience and ultimately support themselves by making money," said Twitch Chief Product Officer Mike Minton. The release of the latest Grand Theft Auto title could draw so much attention that its impact will be felt beyond just the world of gaming. BambooHR, a workplace time-off platform, reported that paid time off requests for the "GTA VI" release date are nearly 13% higher than equivalent days in 2024 and 2025. It also noted that nearly one in five workers are planning to take time off for the launch. PwC issued a report examining all the different sectors of the economy that could benefit from the game's launch — or be hurt by it. The firm projected that food delivery companies could see a surge from hunkered-down gamers, and Miami tourism could benefit. PwC noted that foreign visitors to Seoul's Bukchon Hanok Village, which inspired a location in the hit Netflix movie KPop Demon Hunters, increased 118% in the four weeks following the movie's debut. Music streaming also looks set to get a boost. Tom Petty's "Love Is a Long Road," which appeared in the first "GTA VI" trailer in December 2023, reportedly saw Spotify streams jump by more than 37,000%. On the downside, the game could distract from movies and streaming entertainment. "How are people spending Thanksgiving? There's a lot of sports on TV, but you've also got a pretty solid group of your demographics that are going to be focused on playing 'GTA VI,'" said Bart Spiegel, who leads PwC's Global Entertainment & Media sector. "You're going to start to pull eyeballs away from video streaming platforms. "I think you're going to hear a lot of analyst calls in the first quarter of 2027 saying, 'Hey, listen, some of our numbers were down because of the release of this game,'" Spiegel added. Rockstar Games declined CNBC's interview request. Watch the video above to learn more.

articles.content: Watch: What we know so far about the Microsoft outage A major Microsoft outage has impacted schools, healthcare systems, businesses, courts and governments around the world. Services including Teams, Outlook and AI software Copilot, are being restored almost 24 hours since issues first surfaced. Microsoft said the outage was not a cyber-security incident and was caused by a technical issue. It has apologised for the disruption. Here's what we know about the services affected and what went wrong. Some Microsoft 365 services have been affected by "connectivity problems" with problems reported in at least 74 countries. From late on Thursday, customers reported varying levels of access - many were unable to send or receive emails, view certain files or details on their calendar apps. But some users were able to use Teams, messaging and online meeting functions without issues. As of Friday afternoon, Microsoft said it had seen "encouraging recovery progress" in Europe and improvement in North America. The company added that it was focused on "addressing the remaining areas of disruption" but warned "some users may still experience intermittent issues". In a later statement, the company said it was continuing to see improvements "with email queues significantly reduced and approaching normal levels". The company attributed the ongoing outage to an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade. "We have addressed the underlying issue and continue to restore service to remaining customers and regions," it said on Friday. Although services are beginning to resume, Microsoft has warned of continued "intermittent access issues", meaning some users will still struggle to load their inboxes and could experience "delayed email delivery". In other words, it is not quite safe to assume every email you send is going to arrive in its intended recipient's inbox right away. Earlier, Microsoft said it would be extending the "timeout window" to 48 hours "to help protect delayed messages as delivery catches up". The email timeout window refers to the amount of time Outlook will wait to receive an email. When they do show up, the timestamp will be when they were delivered rather than when they were sent. Although email service Outlook appears to be resuming, the outage has so far lasted for more than 20 hours - in outage terms that is considered a long time. Prof James Ferryman from the University of Reading's department of computer science said the details the company has disclosed provide some clues. "What Microsoft has told us is that the part of its servers that sets up secure connections is getting swamped, and once that happens the server just stops answering," he said. "The trouble is that this kind of failure snowballs. "One server falls over, its work gets passed to the next one, and meanwhile huge numbers of phones and laptops keep trying to get back in. "You can't just turn it all back on at once. You have to bring it back bit by bit." The challenge is therefore not just fixing the fault, but managing the huge surge of devices trying to reconnect once services start coming back online. Gergely Orosz, a former leading software engineer at several major tech companies including Skype and Uber, said this could be the "most disruptive" business email outage "of all time". He said it was still difficult to know just how many people have been affected by the disruption, but added he "cannot recall" an outage over business email ever taking this long to return to normal. Australian cyber-security expert Troy Hunt told the BBC the outage could have far-reaching consequences. "Microsoft is a massive part of the internet backbone and reminds us how critical email still is. "Not only does this outage affect many people's ability to work but also things like the ability to communicate about appointments, purchase things that need verification, create or access accounts and services," he said. In a statement, Microsoft said it was "deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners. "We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously. We are seeing broad recovery and stability across our services." More than 430 million people use Microsoft 365 apps according to Microsoft's website. The full scale of the outage has not been confirmed. Microsoft 365 is used by companies worldwide and is expected to have a knock-on effect to other services. Tech giants OpenAI and Anthropic both earlier reported problems as a result of the outage. ChatGPT-maker OpenAI said it was investigating an issue affecting its connections to Microsoft's services, which had caused some tools to not work as expected. From city governments in the US to Australian spy agencies, disruption across the globe has been widespread. Courts from Los Angeles to Texas earlier warned that communications might be delayed. In Canada, the public broadcaster CBC reported that a healthcare network running several hospitals in Toronto was experiencing email issues, but that patient care was not affected. The government of Japan also said its shared IT platform had been disrupted. Across the UK, GP surgeries, pharmacies, police and schools have been affected by the outage. Some GP surgeries had urged patients not to submit messages via their website while police forces were also earlier asking the public to call if they want to make a report. articles.title: SpaceX Launches Fifteenth Starship to Solidify Monopolistic Orbital Dominance
articles.content: Reuters SpaceX successfully launched its Starship spacecraft on a mission that aimed for both orbit and return Starbase, Texas: SpaceX launched the 15th flight of its Starship spacecraft from Texas on Friday on a mission the company hopes will be the first round-trip rocket voyage to orbit and back to the very spot where it left Earth, a key test of Elon Musk 's effort to build a fully reusable rocket system. Plans call for Starship's uncrewed upper-stage vessel to re-enter the atmosphere after nearly a day in orbit and return to its launch tower on Saturday for an engine-controlled touchdown assisted by the giant mechanical arms of a pioneering catch-landing mechanism. SpaceX had intended to use the same return-flight and "chopstick"-arm technology to recover Starship's lower-stage booster rocket shortly after the two parts of the spacecraft separated within minutes of the launch. But the Super Heavy booster, for reasons not immediately clear, was diverted from its return flight path to a fixed point over the Gulf of Mexico and momentarily hovered in the air before exploding a short distance over the sea surface. SpaceX mission controllers hoped to have better luck in steering Starship's upper stage back to home base at the end of its flight. The vehicle reached orbit about 27 minutes after launch, SpaceX said. Live Events KEY TEST OF REUSABILITY Bringing the top portion of the spacecraft intact back to the platform where it was launched would mark a breakthrough in the ambitions of Musk, who founded SpaceX in 2002, to reduce spaceflight costs by developing a fully recyclable rocket system. The combined vehicle, consisting of the main Starship cargo-and-crew vessel perched atop its Super Heavy booster rocket and standing 40 stories high, roared off its launch pad from SpaceX's South Texas Starbase complex along the Gulf of Mexico near Brownsville. The flight marked Starship's 15th test flight since 2023 and the second to carry a batch of operational Starlink satellites to orbit. That makes the mission both a revenue-generating endeavor for SpaceX's satellite-connectivity business and a high-stakes test for a rocket ship still under development. Starship 15 began releasing its cargo of 26 satellites about 36 minutes into its flight in a payload-delivery operation expected to take less than an hour to complete, the company said in a livestream presentation of the mission. Musk's space and AI business views Starship as key to expanding its network of Starlink internet satellites and, in the future, deploying a swarm of orbital AI data-processing centers dubbed Starmind, as the company positions itself to become a high-tech infrastructure provider. SpaceX last launched Starship in September, taking the rocket and a payload of satellites to orbit for the first time despite some rocket engines shutting down mid-flight. That mission, planned to last 10 hours, ended after roughly three hours with an upper stage splashing down intact into the Pacific Ocean before bursting into flames. RETURN-FLIGHT AND RECOVERY PLANS For Friday's mission, the company was aiming for both the lower-stage Super Heavy and the upper-stage Starship to return to the spacecraft's Texas launch site for safe landing and recovery. Plans called for the orbital cruise vessel to touch down about 22 hours after launch. SpaceX has said it would be a "breakthrough moment in making Starship a reliable, rapidly reusable rocket" if that feat is achieved. SpaceX has previously returned the 236-foot (72-meter) Super Heavy booster three times to its launch pad after sending Starship to space, with the booster flying itself back to Earth minutes after launch and gently descending upright into the grasp of a pair of large mechanical arms fixed to the launch tower. The last such "tower catch" was in March 2025. It was not immediately clear why Friday's attempt failed. Starship was expected to descend from space after completing 14 orbits around Earth, setting up its debut catch landing for Saturday afternoon. Musk has said he expects to achieve a pace of weekly Starship launches by the first half of 2027. NASA has helped fund Starship's development with roughly $3.2 billion since selecting the rocket ship in 2021 to serve as a lunar lander for its astronauts under the multibillion-dollar Artemis moon program. SpaceX has put at least $15 billion of its own funds into the rocket's development. NASA and SpaceX expect Starship to land humans on the moon by 2028, though several major testing objectives remain that analysts and industry engineers believe will push that timeline back. Those milestones include demonstrating complex fuel transfers between Starship tanker rockets in orbit, a critical process that will enable Starship to travel beyond Earth's orbit to the moon. Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin is also developing a moon lander, Blue Moon, for NASA under the Artemis program. Blue Moon is poised to join Starship and another spacecraft, NASA's Orion capsule, in Earth's orbit next year for Artemis III, a docking test mission before NASA's planned moon landing missions begin with Artemis IV. Isku pysäyttää kohtauksen saaneen sydämessä riehuvan sähköisen myrskyn, mikä käynnistää sydämen ja palauttaa sitä normaaliin lyöntitahtiin. Laite myös neuvoo koko ajan elvyttäjää. Jyväskylän yliopistossa laadittu ohjelma analysoi sydämen tilaa ja tekee analyysin perusteella nopean päätöksen iskun antamisesta. Avaa kuvien katselu Teemu Paloniemi kuuli sydäniskurihankkeesta ensimmäistä kertaa ainejärjestönsä tiloissa toiselta opiskelijalta. Kuva: Timo Hytönen / Yle Paloniemi arvostaa erityisesti sitä, että iskurihankkeessa hän pääsi harjoittelemaan tavoitteellista ohjelmointia, jota yliopistossa muutoin ei olisi päässyt tekemään. – Olen oppinut laadukkaan, vakavan ja täsmällisen ohjelmoinnin taitoa.
